common_name: Campfield Apple (Historic Newark New Jersey Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while still dormant in early spring, in full sun on well-drained soil; Campfield is vigorous and tolerates the light, sandy soils common to its native New Jersey.

directions: Campfield was one of the two principal varieties, alongside Harrison, that built the reputation of Newark's famous colonial and Federal-era cider trade in Essex County, New Jersey. The small, hard, russeted fruit is too astringent and dry for fresh eating, but blended with sweeter juice it contributes acidity, tannin, and good keeping qualities to a cider must. Early American pomologists such as William Coxe described it among the region's named cider apples by the early 1800s, though it had largely vanished from commerce by the 20th century. Grow it as a dedicated cidermaking variety on a vigorous rootstock, since the fruit holds little value for dessert use.
sources: William Coxe, A View of the Cultivation of Fruit Trees (1817)
S.A. Beach, The Apples of New York (1905)
Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Blue Pearmain Apple (Old New England Roadside Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Blue Pearmain tolerates the thin, rocky soils and harsh winters typical of its native New England hill country.

directions: Blue Pearmain is a large, coarse-grained New England apple with dull purple-red skin overlaid with a waxy grey-blue bloom, long grown along old stone-walled farm lanes and pastures of Massachusetts, Vermont, and Maine. Henry David Thoreau praised it in his 1862 essay 'Wild Apples' as one of the hardiest, most weather-beaten fruits of the New England roadside, and farmsteads commonly pressed its abundant juice into cider as well as storing the fruit for winter keeping. The flesh is mild, slightly dry, and only moderately sweet, which made it more valued historically for cider and baking than for fresh eating. The tree is notably cold-hardy and tolerant of poor soil, qualities that let it persist on abandoned homesteads long after cultivation ceased.
sources: Henry David Thoreau, 'Wild Apples' (The Atlantic Monthly, 1862)
S.A. Beach, The Apples of New York (1905)

common_name: Hightop Sweeting Apple (Colonial New England Sweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Hightop Sweeting is an upright, vigorous grower that establishes readily on a standard seedling rootstock.

directions: Hightop Sweeting is among the oldest named apple varieties in North America, grown in New England dooryards since the colonial era, well before most other American-origin cultivars had been selected and named. True to its name, the small to medium yellow fruit is intensely sweet with almost no acidity, and colonial farmers prized its low-acid juice for blending into cider to raise the sugar content of the must before fermentation, as well as for fresh eating, baking, and livestock feed. The tree tends to grow tall and upright, hence 'hightop,' and bears reliably once established. It survives today mainly in heirloom orchard collections and living-history sites rather than commercial cultivation.
sources: S.A. Beach, The Apples of New York (1905)

common_name: Granite Beauty Apple (New Hampshire Heritage Dual-Purpose Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Granite Beauty benefits from a vigorous rootstock since it can be a light, irregular bearer.

directions: Granite Beauty was discovered in the early 19th century in southern New Hampshire and has long been considered one of the state's signature heirloom apples, prized for its richly aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh with hints of fennel or anise beneath a thin, waxy, mottled red-and-yellow skin. Though delicious fresh, it was historically valued just as much as a cider apple, since its complex flavor and good sugar content made for an aromatic, well-balanced juice. The variety fell out of commercial favor because the tree bears irregularly and the fruit bruises and spots easily, but heritage orchardists in northern New England have kept it in cultivation. Give it full sun, good air circulation, and expect a light bearer that rewards patience with exceptional flavor.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

common_name: Vandevere Apple (Early Delaware Valley Dual-Purpose Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Vandevere is a moderately vigorous tree traditionally grown in the mid-Atlantic without specialized care.

directions: Vandevere is an early American apple traced to the Vandevere family of the Wilmington, Delaware area, grown since at least the late 1700s in the mid-Atlantic region. Nineteenth-century pomologists noted that the name had been applied somewhat inconsistently to more than one similar variety across different orchards and states, a common hazard with old, widely propagated regional apples spread by grafted scionwood rather than formal registries. Where the true old Delaware Vandevere persisted, it was valued as a crisp, tart, yellow-skinned apple good for cooking and cider alike, ripening in fall and keeping reasonably well into winter. It is grown today only by heirloom orchardists working to sort out and preserve the old mid-Atlantic apple lineages.
sources: S.A. Beach, The Apples of New York (1905)
